title: Eliza Fowler Beaman
summary: Eliza Fowler Beaman was a storyteller, plant-knowledge contributor, Southampton schoolteacher, and public community participant whose surviving record connects Montaukett and Shinnecock histories while leaving important family details unresolved.
content:
Eliza Fowler Beaman, also recorded as Elizabeth Fowler Beaman, appears in family photographs, Shinnecock pageant records, and collections of Long Island Indigenous stories and plant knowledge. The reviewed sources do not provide verified birth or death dates, but they preserve her own work as a storyteller, knowledge contributor, Southampton schoolteacher, and participant in public community gatherings.1

A family record with unresolved captions

Around 1910, Eliza was photographed with Anthony Beaman and George Lewis Fowler Sr. Captions reproduced on the same page of The History and Archaeology of the Montauk disagree about whether George was her father or grandfather. A separate caption describes a possible 1905 wedding photograph of Eliza and Anthony, but the date is marked as uncertain and no ceremony location is given. This profile keeps those conflicts visible rather than selecting a relationship, date, or place that the source does not resolve.2

Stories and plant knowledge

Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians records that Eliza and Anthony Beaman supplied five tales and contributed plant knowledge. The volume connects Eliza with knowledge about wild cherry, boneset, sweet fern, tansy, blackberry root, tobacco, and wild mustard. These records are presented as historical evidence of knowledge sharing, not as medical instructions.3

Teacher and pageant participant

A 1914 Shinnecock pageant record names “Elizabeth Fowler Beaman” among the participants and identifies her as a teacher in the Southampton School. The pageant was a historical presentation and should not be confused with the living Shinnecock Powwow tradition. The record adds a documented public role to Eliza’s story while also showing how community members were represented in early twentieth-century pageant programs.4

Springy Banks in 1944

On September 24, 1944, a source places Eliza with Anthony Beaman and other Native participants at an intertribal gathering at Springy Banks in East Hampton. The gathering belongs to a wider period when Native people from Long Island and neighboring communities used public events to sustain relationships and affirm continuing presence.5

Reading the surviving record

The surviving sources connect Eliza with both Montaukett and Shinnecock family and community histories, but they do not provide a complete life history. This profile therefore withholds vital dates, does not resolve the daughter-or-granddaughter caption conflict, and does not merge her with similarly named Fowler family members.

Reading the map

The map chronology connects the broad public Shinnecock Reservation context for the 1914 pageant with the public Springy Banks site in 1944. The line orders documented records by date; it is not a reconstruction of Eliza’s exact travel route or private residence.

References

  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), p. 376.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), p. 345.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, vol. IV (1980), pp. 115 and 119–121.
why_this_matters: Eliza Fowler Beaman’s record preserves a woman’s own contributions to storytelling, plant knowledge, education, and public community life. Keeping the gaps and conflicting captions visible also shows how responsibly written history can honor a person without inventing a complete biography.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported profile of Eliza Fowler Beaman with her storytelling and plant-knowledge contributions, teaching role, public gatherings, and a two-stop chronology that preserves unresolved family-caption conflicts.
